claims.text: The solutionized and annealed Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy has a homogeneous solid-solution microstructure.
The initial Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy has a stable short-range-order configuration.
Tensile deformation at temperatures from 100 to 700 K and a strain rate near 10^-3 s^-1 dynamically alters SRO in Co-free FeNiCrMn.
Deformation-induced SRO evolution may include formation, modification, or dissolution of local chemical order.
Stress and temperature dynamically modify SRO during deformation.
Dynamic SRO modification temporarily increases local obstacles to dislocation motion.
SRO-mediated modulation of dislocation mobility enhances yield strength.
The proposed SRO-mediated strengthening occurs without sacrificing ductility.
A specific temperature and strain-rate window within the tested regime produces both enhanced yield strength and enhanced ductility relative to the static baseline.
Changes in diffraction peak position, width, or intensity can track deformation-associated structural evolution.
The specified neutron-diffraction observables are direct indicators of SRO changes in this alloy.
In situ TEM chemical mapping can confirm local ordering or compositional variations concurrent with dislocation behavior.
A strain rate near 10^-3 s^-1 is a regime in which dynamic deformation phenomena have been reported in a related CoCrFeMnNi alloy.
The proposed mechanism is bounded to solutionized and annealed Co-free FeNiCrMn under tensile loading near 10^-3 s^-1 and 100–700 K.
The baseline is an undeformed state with stable SRO and no modulation of dislocation mobility by dynamic chemical reordering.
Concurrent deformation mechanisms may complicate attribution of mechanical changes to SRO evolution.
Failure to detect statistically significant SRO changes by both methods, or failure of detected changes to correlate with strength and ductility, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The proposed comparator is an undeformed static state, yet yield strength and ductility require deformation to measure. Thus it is not a mechanically matched baseline for deciding whether dynamic SRO evolution improves the strength–ductility balance.

The mediator allows SRO dissolution, while the mechanism generally assigns SRO modification an obstacle-increasing and strengthening effect. The cited evidence instead indicates that SRO destruction can produce glide-plane softening, so the direction of the mechanism is not consistently specified.
